summary: Introductory partner discovery between Redwood and Aurora Integrations to explore GPU/cloud partnership and potential marketplace + integration pilot. Covered high-level architecture, hosting modes (hosted, dedicated, private/VPC), security/compliance needs, benchmarking plan, and GTM motions. Agreed on follow-ups: share partner deck, benchmark scripts, and schedule SE deep-dive for private/VPC performance tests.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood, and with me is Samir, our solutions engineer, and Ana from partnerships. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya Chen: Hi Jordan, thanks. I'm Maya, I run partnerships at Aurora Integrations. We also have Liam and Ravi and Ellen on the call.
[00:18] Liam O'Connor: Hey folks.
[00:20] Ravi Patel: Morning all.
[00:22] Ana Gomez: Great to meet you all.
[00:25] Jordan Lee: Awesome. We're here to do a quick partner intro and discovery — understand Aurora's cloud + GPU offering, see where Redwood could fit in, and figure out pilot ideas and next steps. Maya, can you give a quick overview of Aurora?
[00:38] Maya Chen: Sure. Aurora is focused on managed GPU clusters and a marketplace that pairs customers with curated infra partners. We support bare metal and cloud-backed fleets, and we're seeing a lot of demand for inference serving and turnkey stacks for LLMs. We're exploring vendor partnerships to provide a first-class inference experience.
[00:54] Samir Patel: Nice. Does Aurora do any managed model serving today or is it infra-only?
[00:58] Maya Chen: Mostly infra and orchestration. We have some early-stage managed offerings but customers ask for opinionated inference runtimes, cost predictability, and simpler batching/caching out-of-the-box. That's the ask driving partner conversations.
[01:12] Jordan Lee: That aligns a lot with what Redwood does — we provide a serving runtime plus control plane for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. We focus on latency, cost, and developer experience. For partners, there's typically a few angles: 1) list Redwood as a curated model serving option on Aurora marketplace, 2) joint integration where Aurora manages the infra and Redwood provides the runtime, or 3) co-marketed pilot for a customer.
[01:33] Liam O'Connor: For the joint integration, how are networking and tenancy handled? We need to know about VPC peering, private control plane options.
[01:40] Samir Patel: We have a Private deployment option — a customer-managed VPC with a private control plane, and we also offer an on-prem package for air-gapped environments. VPC peering and transit are supported, and we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key management.
[01:55] Ellen Zhou: On security, can you speak to audit logs, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and SOC 2?
[02:01] Jordan Lee: Yes — Redwood supports SSO and SAML, granular RBAC, and audit logs. We're SOC 2 aligned and have enterprise security docs we can share. For high-compliance customers we offer private deployments and additional contract terms.
[02:13] Ravi Patel: Great. On the infra side we care about predictable throughput. If we offer shared pools to multiple customers, we need to understand per-tenant isolation and burst handling. Also curious about model quantization and how that affects latency/cost.
[02:27] Samir Patel: Our runtime is GPU-optimized and supports quantization-friendly execution paths. We do continuous batching and KV cache for prefixes; that helps reduce per-token cost for chatty workloads. For isolation, Dedicated pools give reserved capacity and predictable throughput; we can also do tenancy controls on top of that.
[02:44] Maya Chen: When you say KV cache, is that per-customer? How do cache invalidation and cold-starts work?
[02:51] Samir Patel: Good question. KV cache is per-server and can be configured per-tenant. We surface controls for prefix caching, TTLs, and automated invalidation hooks. Cold-starts are mitigated with warm pools and burst capacity — configurable in Dedicated.
[03:06] Jordan Lee: From a partner perspective, many Aurora customers are trying to balance latency vs cost; we typically recommend a mix of hosted for dev and proofs-of-concept, and Dedicated/Private for production with SLAs. That gives a clear upsell path: start hosted, then reserve capacity.
[03:23] Liam O'Connor: Do you provide performance profiles or benchmarks for common models — e.g., Llama variants, Mistral, etc?
[03:29] Samir Patel: Yes; we maintain a model catalog with curated open models and performance profiles. We'll share benchmark scripts and sample config for quantization and kernel selection. We also have a small benchmarking harness customers can run in their environment.
[03:43] Maya Chen: Would you expect Aurora to run Redwood-managed control plane or the private control plane?
[03:48] Jordan Lee: Both are possible. For marketplace listings we often start with our hosted API so customers can try quickly. For deeper integration Aurora can run a private deployment and Redwood will provide the runtime and ops tooling. That said, some partners prefer Redwood-hosted endpoints with network restrictions while the marketplace handles billing and orchestration.
[04:06] Ravi Patel: Licensing and pricing — what's the partner economics look like? We need an idea of margin and pricing models for listing on marketplace.
[04:13] Jordan Lee: We have usage-based pricing for hosted (per-token/per-embed), reserved capacity contracts for Dedicated, and enterprise licensing for Private. For partners we typically provide a partner pricing sheet and revenue share models — Jordan to share the deck with details.
[04:27] Ana Gomez: Onboarding — how long does a pilot take? If Aurora wants to run a performance pilot on a subset of customers, what's the typical timeline?
[04:35] Samir Patel: For a standard benchmark and pilot, if you can provide an infra test account and 1-2 sample prompt sets, we can run an initial throughput/latency baseline within 1-2 weeks and recommended configs within 2-3 weeks. Private/VPC pilots are longer — usually 3-6 weeks depending on networking and compliance reviews.
[04:56] Maya Chen: Good to know. For the marketplace, we'd like to surface a demo or quickstart so customers can try Redwood-backed inference. Is there a light integration path?
[05:05] Jordan Lee: Yes — we have a quickstart flow and sample Docker/Helm charts for private installs plus a hosted trial for immediate demos. We'll share the quickstart and the marketplace onboarding checklist.
[05:16] Liam O'Connor: From a technical angle, do you support tool-calling / function calling or structured output? Some of our customers want reliable JSON outputs for downstream systems.
[05:25] Samir Patel: We support streaming responses, tool/function calling primitives, and structured output helpers. We also do post-processing hooks and can integrate with event sinks for results.
[05:36] Ravi Patel: Any limits on sequence length or special considerations for long context? KV cache helps but for retrieval-augmented workflows we'd need to know how you manage long contexts.
[05:45] Samir Patel: We have a few strategies: chunking + KV cache, compressed KV caching heuristics, and model variants with extended context support. We can recommend kernel selection and memory configs based on your workload.
[05:57] Maya Chen: On the commercial side, are there co-sell or referral programs? Aurora is interested in go-to-market collaboration if the tech lines up.
[06:04] Jordan Lee: Absolutely. We do co-sell and referral programs; we can include joint marketing assets and co-branded pages on the marketplace. Ana will coordinate GTM assets.
[06:13] Ana Gomez: Yep I'll follow up with a GTM checklist and sample collateral.
[06:18] Maya Chen: A few security follow-ups: encryption at rest details, key rotation, and whether Redwood can integrate with our HSM. Also ISO/SOC attestation docs.
[06:28] Ellen Zhou: Also logging retention — some of our customers need 12-24 months of audit logs, and we need to know how that works with hosted offerings.
[06:36] Jordan Lee: We support KMS/HSM integrations and can do envelope encryption. Audit log retention is configurable; for hosted customers we offer log export and long-term storage add-ons. We'll share the security pack.
[06:48] Samir Patel: For private installs we can be flexible on retention and where logs live since you're managing the infra.
[06:54] Ravi Patel: For benchmarking, what metrics will you collect? We need CPU/GPU utilization, p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens.
[07:03] Samir Patel: We'll capture those metrics and provide a per-run spreadsheet with cost estimates. We'll also surface kernel selection notes and memory utilization so you can tune instance types.
[07:14] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Any quick blockers or red flags on our side?
[07:18] Jordan Lee: Not at this stage; the main items are security docs, infra test account, and sample prompt sets. From there we can run a baseline.
[07:27] Liam O'Connor: Regarding multi-tenant use, if Aurora wants to offer Redwood as a managed option to multiple end customers, is there support for tenant-level metering and per-customer billing?
[07:36] Samir Patel: Yes — we surface per-customer metering and token-level breakdowns. Integration with billing systems is done via the marketplace or via APIs depending on the model.
[07:46] Maya Chen: OK I'd like to propose a pilot: we provide an infra test account, a representative prompt set, and one early adopter customer. Redwood runs a 2-week benchmark and returns configs and cost estimates. If that looks good we scope integration.
[07:59] Jordan Lee: That works. We'll scope the pilot and Samir will run the bench. We'll also include a private deployment option if you want to test VPC flow.
[08:08] Ana Gomez: I'll coordinate the GTM and assets piece after we validate technical fit.
[08:13] Maya Chen: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[08:16] Jordan Lee: Recap: Jordan sends partner deck and pricing matrix; Samir shares benchmark scripts and quickstart; Maya to confirm pilot stakeholders and share infra test account; schedule SE deep-dive for private/VPC networking and performance.
[08:33] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email.
[08:36] Liam O'Connor: Thanks all.
[08:38] Ravi Patel: Thanks.
[08:39] Ellen Zhou: Bye.
[08:41] Jordan Lee: Thanks team, talk soon.

Notes: Transcription has minor errors and speaker overlap in places.
